You must be able to describe and compare the development methodologies:

  • iterative development process
  • agile methodologies
Recap

docs.title: The Software Development Lifecycle
docs.text:
The Software Development Lifecycle is generally an iterative process that consists of six stages:

  • Analysis - to fully understand the problem and what the program must do
  • Design - to plan how the program will work before building it
  • Implementation - to write the actual code
  • Testing - to check that the program works correctly and meets the requirements
  • Documentation - to produce materials that help users and future developers understand and use the software.
  • Evaluation - to judge how successful the software is

docs.title: The Waterfall Method
docs.text:
A traditional method of software development is called the Waterfall Method.

The Waterfall Method is classified as a linear development process, as the developer or development team works through each stage sequentially with little to no involvement from the client until the final product is delivered.

Although it is classified as a linear development process, in practice it is often necessary to revisit earlier stages. For example, if an issue is discovered during testing, the team may need to go back and revise the design, reimplement it, and test it again.

In the early days of software engineering, this process made sense.

However, it is rarely used in modern software development due to its lack of flexibility.

In the real world, many developers use Agile methods.

Task One: Waterfall Analysis

A company is developing software to control traffic lights across a city.

  1. Describe one advantage of using the Waterfall Model for this project.
  2. Describe one disadvantage of using the Waterfall Model for this project.
  3. Explain why the advantage you identified is particularly important for this type of software.
  4. Evaluate whether Waterfall is the most suitable methodology for this project.

In your answer:

  • Consider reliability.
  • Consider client requirements.
  • Consider changes during development.
  • Reach a justified conclusion.

docs.title: Agile Methods
docs.text:
Agile is considered more flexible than traditional iterative methods.

Instead of following a rigid sequence of stages, Agile breaks the project down into smaller, manageable units of work based on what the client needs known as User Stories.

Each of these User Stories are included in the overal Software Development Plan. The Software Development Plan will also idnetify the timescale for which each User Story should be completed.

Teams of developers will work in shorts “sprints” to produce working prototypes which can be tested by the client.

Each sprint typically lasts one to four weeks and involves a cycle of planning, design, implementation, and testing. This approach allows teams to produce working software early and update it frequently based on feedback.

A key benefit of Agile is its emphasis on collaboration and adaptability. Stakeholders, including clients and end-users, are involved throughout the development process, not just at the beginning or end. This ongoing communication helps ensure that the software continues to meet the users’ needs as they evolve.

By regularly reassessing priorities and making improvements at each step, Agile teams can respond to changes quickly—something that is much harder to do with more traditional methods like Waterfall. As a result, Agile has become one of the most widely adopted methodologies in modern software development.

Task Two: Understanding Iteration

A client requests a mobile app for ordering food.

  1. Explain what is meant by iteration in software development.
  2. Describe how the software might move between:
    • Design and Implementation
    • Implementation and Testing
  3. Explain why iteration can improve the final product.
  4. A client requests a major change after testing has begun. Explain how:
    • Waterfall would deal with this change.
    • Agile would deal with this change.
  5. Which approach would be more effective? Justify your answer.

docs.title: Advantages/Disadvantages
docs.text:
Waterfall MethodAgile Methodology Advantages

The Waterfall model is well suited to large-scale projects and big development teams, especially when there is a long lead time. Since the client is usually less involved once development begins, they must clearly define their requirements at the start, as this forms part of the legally binding contract.

This model focuses more on producing high-quality software than on rapid development. As a result, the software tends to be thoroughly tested and contains fewer bugs. Projects using the Waterfall approach are often completed on schedule and within budget.

Setting clear milestones at the beginning of the project helps both the development team and the client monitor progress more easily.

Disadvantages

One of the main drawbacks of the Waterfall model is its rigid, step-by-step structure, which makes it difficult to change the plan once development has started. Since client input is usually only gathered at the beginning of the project, they are not involved throughout. This means that if the client is unsure about what they need at the start or if their requirements change during the project, the final software may not meet their expectations.

Another issue is that once the software reaches the testing stage, making changes can be challenging. If updates are needed at that point, it can take extra time and increase costs.

To reduce this problem, it can help to involve clients at key points during the project so that adjustments can be made earlier in the process.

Advantages

Agile is ideal for smaller projects, such as developing or regularly updating apps, and works well with small development teams. The client is actively involved throughout the entire development process, and regular feedback is gathered.

This close collaboration helps ensure that the final product closely matches what the client wants, even if their initial requirements were unclear. Agile also offers flexibility—if the client changes their mind or wants to add new features, these changes can usually be made without too much difficulty.

Disadvantages

The Agile methodology has several drawbacks. Initially, there's often no formal, legally binding contract, which can be problematic given the evolving nature of client requirements. Furthermore, Agile is not well-suited for extensive projects or large teams. Clients must also be ready to dedicate significant time to the project, as their continuous involvement is essential.

Another major disadvantage lies in the stringent sprint deadlines, which can lead to incomplete projects. In such cases, the client may face increased costs to finalize the project, or they might have to accept a deliverable with a considerably reduced scope. The frequent updates inherent in Agile can also be challenging to monitor and necessitate rigorous version control for each iteration or update.

docs.title: Iterative vs. Agile Development Processes (Key Points Comparison)
docs.text:
Iterative Agile Client Interaction The client is usually involved only at the analysis and evaluation stages. There is little to no client input during design, implementation, and testing phases. Agile encourages frequent client feedback throughout the project. Ongoing collaboration helps shape the product and ensures it meets client needs. Teamwork Separate teams handle different phases independently, such as design, implementation, and testing. Communication between teams can be limited, potentially causing delays if issues arise. Agile teams are cross-functional and collaborative, combining designers, developers, and testers who work together continuously with rapid communication and shared goals. Documentation Relies on a single, detailed project specification created at the start, which guides the entire project. Changes late in the project can be costly. Minimizes formal documentation, favouring lightweight, flexible documents created as needed. Focus is on working software and communication over paperwork. Measurement of Progress Progress is measured by completing each phase in order, with the final product delivered at the end for client evaluation. Progress is measured by how quickly features are delivered and demonstrated. Agile teams deliver working software regularly with frequent client feedback. Adaptive vs Predictive Iterative development is more predictive, relying on detailed upfront planning and following a set sequence of phases. Agile is highly adaptive, embracing change and continuously adjusting based on feedback and testing throughout the project. Testing Testing happens mainly after implementation in a distinct phase, often late in the process, risking discovering problems late. Testing is continuous and integrated throughout development. Each part is tested as it is built, reducing costly late fixes. Tasks Four and Five: Case Studies

Task Four - Case Study: Microsoft

Microsoft is developing a new version of Windows.

  1. Recommend a development methodology.
  2. Analyse how the methodology would support:
    • large development teams
    • testing
    • customer feedback
    • changing requirements
  3. Evaluate whether the alternative methodology could still be used successfully.
  4. Explain what problems could occur if Microsoft used the alternative methodology.

Task Five - Case Study: Small Business

A medium-sized company requires a payroll system. The requirements are well understood, but legislation may change during development.

  1. Recommend a methodology.
  2. Justify your choice.
  3. Explain why the alternative methodology might still be appropriate.
  4. Reach a conclusion.

docs.title: Agile Methodologies
docs.text:
Agile methodologies generally follow the same development stages (Analysis, Design, Implementation, Testing, Documentation, Evaluation, and Maintenance) but approach them more flexibly. The focus is on quickly getting started while allowing movement between stages as needed. This iterative process enables collaboration between different developer teams, allowing the project’s requirements and solution to evolve step by step.

The Agile methodology places a strong emphasis on teamwork, with regular interaction among developers and frequent engagement with clients or users to create prototypes.

By showing working prototypes as the system develops, teams can gather real-time feedback, allowing for adjustments and improvements throughout the process.

Key Point

A key aspect of agile methodologies is their ability to respond to change, recognizing that requirements are often fluid and that software projects are inherently dynamic.

Rapid Application Development (RAD) is one such example of an agile approach to software and information system creation. Its primary goal is to implement solutions quickly, minimizing upfront planning. RAD involves producing incremental versions or prototypes to refine requirements and address issues as they arise.

While RAD can significantly reduce development time, it may lead to an overemphasis on the Graphical User Interface (GUI) rather than the core functionality of the software. Continuous iteration can also result in a disorganized process, increased errors, and long-term maintenance challenges. Therefore, RAD is best suited for smaller, dynamic projects like apps or websites, but is less ideal for large-scale or mission-critical systems.

docs.title: The Iterative Development Process (Waterfall Model)
docs.text:
The Waterfall model is a structured, linear approach to software development. In this methodology, the stages followed include analysis, design, implementation, testing, documentation, evaluation, and maintenance. Although the process is often referred to as iterative because stages can be revisited, one of its main challenges is that these stages are followed sequentially.

As development progresses, new ideas and requirements will often emerge that were not foreseen during the initial planning stages. This leads to the need to revisit earlier phases of the project to address new issues and correct errors which slows the development process considerably.

As a result, the Waterfall model is often criticized for being overly rigid, slow, and dependent on excessive documentation as each step strictly follows the last.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
What you need to know

You must be able to identify the:

  • purpose

  • scope

  • boundaries

  • functional requirements

of a problem that relates to the design and implementation at this level, in terms of:

  • inputs

  • processes

  • outputs

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The Purpose is a really important part of the analysis stage. It’s all about clearly stating what the software is meant to do – basically, what problem it’s solving or what task it needs to complete.

A clear purpose helps everyone involved understand what the end goal is, and it makes sure the rest of the project stays on track.

In addition, it also helps when you’re thinking about what the program will need to take in (inputs), what it will do (processes), and what it should produce (outputs).

If the purpose isn’t clear, it’s easy for the software to end up doing the wrong thing or not meeting the user’s needs. A good purpose is simple, focused, and makes it easy to check if the final product works the way it’s supposed to.

The SQA define purpose as a general description of the software. At Higher, this should explain what the system is designed to achieve rather than listing every feature in detail.

This is often summarised using the IPO model:

  • Inputs – What information the program receives
  • Processes – What the program does with that information
  • Outputs – What the program produces or displays

This model helps developers stay focused on what the software is meant to do, and it links closely to the functional requirements.

docs.title: Purpose Example
docs.text:
Problem: A school library wants a system to manage book loans.

Purpose: To allow library staff to record when books are borrowed and returned, and to display information about current loans.

Notice that the purpose gives a general overview of the system rather than a detailed list of every feature.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
The Scope is where you set the boundaries of what the software will and won’t do.

Once the purpose is clear, the scope builds on that by outlining exactly what features or tasks will be included in the project – and just as importantly, what’s being left out.

This helps keep the project realistic and manageable, especially if there are time or resource limits. It also stops feature creep, where new ideas get added in along the way and make everything more complicated.

A clear scope gives everyone – from developers to users – a shared understanding of what to expect, which makes planning and development much smoother.

docs.title: Scope Example
docs.text:
For the school library system:

Included in the scope: - Record book loans - Record returned books - Search for books - Display current loans

Not included in the scope: - Online book reservations - Automatic email reminders - Stock ordering from suppliers

This helps developers understand exactly what features should be developed within the project.

Exam Tip

In a Higher exam question, you would not normally be expected to write separate Included and Not Included lists.

These have been used here as a teaching strategy to help you visualise the scope of a system and understand where the limits of the project lie.

In an exam, scope is often described in a short paragraph that explains what the system will do.

docs.title: Boundaries
docs.text:
The Boundaries identify what’s outside the system – in other words, the parts the software won’t deal with. While the scope tells us what’s included in the system, boundaries help make it clear where the system ends and where other systems or people take over.

For example, if a program needs information from a database but doesn’t manage the database itself, that database would be outside the boundary.

Setting boundaries is useful because it helps avoid confusion about what the software is responsible for. It also makes it easier to plan and design the system by focusing only on what actually needs to be built.

docs.title: Boundary Example
docs.text:
For the school library system:

  • The system records loans and returns.
  • The librarian is responsible for physically issuing books.
  • The school's email system is responsible for sending any notifications.
  • The school's network infrastructure is managed by IT staff.

These external people and systems sit outside the boundary of the software being developed.

docs.title: Scope vs Boundaries
docs.text:
Many pupils confuse scope and boundaries because both describe limits. However, they focus on different things.

Scope Boundaries Describes what features and functions the software will and will not provide. Describes what people, systems or responsibilities exist outside the software. Focuses on functionality. Focuses on responsibility. The system will not send email notifications. The school's email system is responsible for sending notifications. The system will not manage room bookings. School staff are responsible for allocating rooms.

A useful way to remember the difference is:

  • Scope = What the software does
  • Boundaries = Who or what is outside the software

docs.title: Worked Example: School Club Registration System
docs.text: A school wants a simple system that allows pupils to register for after-school clubs.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: To allow pupils to view available clubs and register for a club. Teachers can view a list of pupils who have signed up.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Included: - Display available clubs - Register a pupil for a club - View attendee lists

Not Included: - User accounts and login systems - Email or text notifications - Room booking management

docs.title: Boundaries
docs.text:
• Teachers are responsible for creating clubs.
  • Pupils are responsible for entering their own details correctly.
  • Any school email system operates outside the software.
  • The system does not manage staffing or room allocations.

docs.title: Functional Requirements
docs.text: Input Process Output                  Enter pupil name                 Select a club                               Validate entered details                 Store registration details                               Display confirmation message                 Display club attendee list

docs.title: Why this is a good Higher answer
docs.text:
• The purpose provides a general description of the system.
  • The scope identifies what features are included and excluded from the system.
  • The boundaries identify responsibilities that sit outside the software.
  • The functional requirements are clearly linked to inputs, processes and outputs (IPO).

docs.title: Analysis Tasks
docs.text:
Use each scenario to identify the program's:

  • purpose
  • boundaries
  • functional requirements, using the IPO model

docs.title: Task 1: Online Game Leaderboard
docs.text:
A server manages the weekly leaderboard for an online game.

Player details

  • Each player must have a nickname between 6 and 15 characters long.
  • Each player must have a profile image.
  • A default silhouette image can be used if no profile image is provided.

Data used by the system

  • Each week, the system reads player experience points and ranks from a text file.

Processing carried out

  • Sort all players by experience score.
  • Select the top 10 players for the leaderboard.
  • Identify the three players whose experience score has improved the most during the week.
  • The three most improved players do not need to appear in the top 10.

Outputs produced

  • Output the nickname, experience score and profile image for the top 10 players.
  • Output the nickname, experience score and profile image for the three most improved players.
  • Store these outputs in separate text files.
  • The text files are then used to generate an interactive graph and table on the game's website.

Questions

(a) State the purpose of this program.

(b) State two boundaries of the program.

(c) Identify the functional requirements for the program, in terms of inputs, processes and outputs.

docs.title: Task 2: Supermarket Self-Scan System
docs.text:
A supermarket introduces a self-scan system that allows customers to use their smartphones while shopping.

Data used by the system

  • Customers scan a QR code on each item.
  • The system matches the QR code to a text file.
  • The text file contains item names, prices and any discounts available that week.

Processing carried out

  • Add the price of each scanned item to the customer's running total.
  • Apply any discounts automatically when the customer reaches the checkout.
  • Generate an itemised bill.
  • Generate a final payment total.

Outputs produced

  • Send the itemised bill to the customer.
  • Send the itemised bill to the store.
  • Send the final payment total to the customer.
  • Send the final payment total to the store.
  • The final payment amount can then be used to charge the customer's debit card.

Questions

(a) State the purpose of this program.

(b) State two boundaries of the program.

(c) Identify the functional requirements for the program, in terms of inputs, processes and outputs.

docs.title: Task 3: Cinema Ticket Booking System
docs.text:
A cinema introduces an online booking system that allows customers to reserve seats for film screenings.

Booking details

  • Customers choose a film, screening time and seat.
  • Customers enter their name and email address.
  • Customers select the number and type of tickets required.

Data used by the system

  • The system reads film titles, screening times, ticket prices and available seats from a database.
  • The system checks whether the selected seats are still available.

Processing carried out

  • Calculate the total cost of the selected tickets.
  • Mark the selected seats as reserved.
  • Generate a booking reference.
  • Store the booking details.

Outputs produced

  • Display a booking confirmation message.
  • Display the booking reference.
  • Send the booking details to the customer by email.
  • Update the list of available seats for the screening.

Questions

(a) State the purpose of this program.

(b) State two boundaries of the program.

(c) Identify the functional requirements for the program, in terms of inputs, processes and outputs.

docs.title: Task 4: Fitness Class Attendance System
docs.text:
A leisure centre uses a system to record attendance at weekly fitness classes.

Class details

  • Staff select the class name and date.
  • Staff enter the names of members who attend.
  • Each class has a maximum number of spaces available.

Data used by the system

  • The system reads class names, dates and maximum class sizes from a text file.
  • The system reads existing member details from a member database.

Processing carried out

  • Check that each entered member exists in the member database.
  • Count the number of members attending each class.
  • Compare the attendance count with the maximum class size.
  • Store the attendance record for the selected class.

Outputs produced

  • Display the number of members who attended.
  • Display a warning if the class is over capacity.
  • Output an attendance list for staff.
  • Save the updated attendance record.

Questions

(a) State the purpose of this program.

(b) State two boundaries of the program.

(c) Identify the functional requirements for the program, in terms of inputs, processes and outputs.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

For Higher Software Design and Development, you must be able to:

  • identify suitable data types and data structures
  • read and create designs using structure diagrams and pseudocode
  • show the top-level design
  • show the data flow in and out of sub-programs
  • show refinements where more detail is needed
  • design user interfaces using wireframes

Design is the planning stage of software development. It turns the analysis into a clear plan for how the solution will be built.

In the Higher assignment, candidates are expected to produce design documentation before implementation begins. Good design helps ensure that the final solution meets all functional requirements and makes the implementation stage easier.

At Higher level, design is mainly about answering four questions:

Question Design feature What are the main parts of the solution? Top-level design What information is passed between those parts? Data flow How does each main part work? Refinements What data and interface will the program use? Data types, structures, and wireframes

docs.title: Turning Analysis into Design
docs.text:
Analysis describes the problem by identifying the:

  • purpose
  • scope
  • boundaries
  • functional requirements
  • inputs, processes, and outputs

Design uses this information to plan how the solution will be organised and built.

For example, if the analysis says a program must read pupil marks, calculate percentages, find the highest percentage, and display the result, these requirements can become top-level design steps:

Step Top-level design 1 Get results 2 Calculate percentages 3 Find position of pupil with top mark 4 Display pupil with top mark

These main steps form the top-level design. Later, data flow and refinements are added to make the design detailed enough to implement.

docs.title: Modular Design
docs.text:
A module is a section of a program that carries out one clear task.

Each module should perform one specific task. This makes the design easier to understand, test, and maintain.

Breaking a program into modules makes it easier to:

  • implement
  • test
  • debug
  • maintain
  • improve later

In the final program, modules are usually implemented as procedures or functions.

docs.title: Higher Design Techniques You Need to Know
docs.text:
Technique Best for showing Commonly used for Structure diagram The modular breakdown of the program Top-level design Pseudocode The algorithmic steps and refinements Refinements and algorithms Wireframe The layout of the user interface Screen and interface design

Structure diagrams and pseudocode can both show top-level design, data flow, and refinements. They simply present the same design information in different ways.

docs.title: Worked Design Example
docs.text:
The example below shows how a simple requirement develops into a design that is ready to implement.

Design stage Example Analysis requirement Calculate and display the average test score Top-level design 1 Get scores2 Calculate average3 Display average Data flow GetScores() -> scoresCalculateAverage(scores) -> averageDisplayAverage(average) Refinement FOR count <- 1 TO 3INPUT score[count]END FOR

The top-level design gives the main modules, the data flow shows what each module passes on, and the refinement adds detail for one module.

docs.title: Data Types and Data Structures
docs.text:
Once the main design is clear, you should choose suitable data types and structures.

These choices affect validation, storage, and how easily the data can be processed.

Data item Suitable type or structure Reason Pupil name String Stores text Test score Integer Stores a whole number Product price Real Stores a decimal number Login successful Boolean Stores true or false List of marks Array of integers Stores several related values Customer details Record Stores different fields about one item

Exam Tip

When asked to create a design, start with the top-level design first.

Then add:

  • data flow
  • refinements
  • suitable data types and structures

Building the design in this order makes it easier to ensure all functional requirements have been covered.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Design turns the analysis into a clear plan for how the program will be built.

A good Higher design should show:

  • the main modules in the solution
  • the data that flows in and out of each module
  • refinements for modules that need more detail
  • suitable data types and data structures
  • a clear user-interface design, where appropriate

By the end of the design stage, another programmer should be able to understand what the solution will do, how it is split into modules, and what data must move between those modules.

docs.title: Structure Diagrams
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

You must be able to read, understand, create, and implement designs using structure diagrams.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
A structure diagram shows how a program is broken into modules.

Each box represents one task. The highest level shows the main parts of the program, and lower levels show how those parts are refined into smaller tasks.

Structure diagrams are useful when you want to see the overall organisation of a program before thinking about detailed code.

docs.title: National 5 to Higher
docs.text:
At National 5, a structure diagram usually shows the main parts of a program.

For example:

Quiz Program
+-- Get answers
+-- Calculate score
+-- Display score

This is useful because it shows the program broken down into smaller tasks.

At Higher, the structure diagram needs to show more design detail. It should make it clear:

  • what the main modules are
  • what data each module needs
  • what data each module produces
  • which modules have been refined into smaller tasks
  • how the modules could become procedures or functions in the final program
National 5 structure diagram Higher structure diagram Shows the main tasks in the program Shows the main modules in the program Focuses on breaking the problem down Also shows data flow between modules May stop at the top-level design Often includes refinements for complex modules Helps plan the order of tasks Helps plan procedures, functions, and parameters

The key difference is that Higher structure diagrams are not just about naming the tasks. They should also show how data moves through the design.

docs.title: Reading a Structure Diagram
docs.text:
When reading a structure diagram, look for:

  • the overall problem at the top
  • the main modules below it
  • any smaller tasks below a module
  • data flow labels or arrows

The example below shows a program that finds and displays the most-downloaded song on a streaming platform.

docs.title: Showing Data Flow
docs.text:
At Higher, data flow can be added to a structure diagram using labels or arrows.

Use:

  • IN for data passed into a module
  • OUT for data passed out of a module

For a more detailed explanation of what counts as data flow, see Data Flow In and Out.

docs.title: Data Flow Tables
docs.text:
If the diagram becomes crowded, the same information can be shown in a table.

Tables are often clearer when several arrays or variables move between modules.

docs.title: Showing Refinements
docs.text:
A refinement breaks a module into smaller tasks.

You use refinements when a module is too broad and needs more detail before it could be implemented.

The smaller tasks below the module show how that module will work. They do not need to be full program code.

At Higher, refinements are useful because a top-level module may be too general on its own. Breaking it into smaller steps makes the design clearer for the programmer.

For example, a module called Find most-downloaded song might be refined into:

Find most-downloaded song
+-- Set top position to first song
+-- Loop through remaining songs
+-- Compare current downloads with top downloads
+-- Update top position if current song is higher

This gives enough detail to understand the logic, but it still stays at the design stage.

You do not need to refine every module. A module only needs refinement if the task is complex or unclear.

docs.title: Check Your Diagram
docs.text:
A good Higher structure diagram should make these questions easy to answer:

  • What are the main modules?
  • What data does each module need?
  • What data does each module produce?
  • Which modules have been refined?
  • Could the modules become procedures or functions?

Higher exam tip

If your diagram only lists the main tasks, it may look more like a National 5 answer.

To make it stronger for Higher, add data flow and refinements where they are needed.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Structure diagrams show how a program is broken into modules.

At National 5, a structure diagram often shows the main tasks in a program. At Higher, it should show more design detail, especially data flow and refinements.

A good Higher structure diagram should show:

  • the main modules in the program
  • any smaller tasks used to refine complex modules
  • the data that goes into each module
  • the data that comes out of each module
  • how the modules could become procedures or functions

The key difference is that a Higher structure diagram should not just list tasks. It should help another programmer understand how the solution is organised and what data moves between the parts of the program.

docs.title: Pseudocode
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

You must be able to read, understand, create, and implement designs written in pseudocode.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Pseudocode is a way of designing an algorithm using structured English instead of a specific programming language.

It is not finished program code. It is a design that explains the logic clearly enough for a programmer to implement later.

At Higher, pseudocode is used to show:

  • the main algorithm, also called the top-level design
  • data flow in and out of modules
  • refinements for modules that need more detail
  • important loops, decisions, and calculations

docs.title: National 5 to Higher
docs.text:
At National 5, pseudocode often focuses on the steps needed to solve a problem.

At Higher, pseudocode needs to show more design detail. It should make clear how the solution is split into modules and what data moves between them.

National 5 pseudocode Higher pseudocode Shows the steps in an algorithm Shows the top-level design and refinements May focus on one sequence of instructions Is usually split into modules May not show data flow Should show IN and OUT data flow Helps plan the logic Helps plan procedures, functions, and parameters

The key difference is that Higher pseudocode should show the structure of the solution, not just a list of instructions.

docs.title: Main Algorithm
docs.text:
The main algorithm shows the major steps of the solution.

It should list the main tasks in a logical order without adding every small programming detail.

For example:

1 Get results
2 Calculate percentages
3 Find position of pupil with top mark
4 Display pupil with top mark

Each main step represents a module. In the final program, these modules could become procedures or functions.

docs.title: Adding Data Flow
docs.text:
At Higher, each main step should show the data it needs and the data it produces.

This is often shown with the pseudocode on the left and the data flow on the right.

Use:

  • IN for data passed into a module
  • OUT for data passed out of a module
Pseudocode Data flow 1 Get results OUT: pupilName(), prelimMark(), courseMark() 2 Calculate percentages IN: prelimMark(), courseMark()OUT: percentage() 3 Find position of pupil with top mark IN: percentage()OUT: topPosition 4 Display pupil with top mark IN: pupilName(), percentage(), topPosition

The brackets in names such as pupilName() and percentage() show that they are arrays.

For more help deciding what should be IN or OUT, see Data Flow In and Out.

docs.title: Adding Refinements
docs.text:
A refinement breaks one main step into smaller steps.

You use a refinement when a main step is too broad and needs more detail before it could be implemented.

The numbering shows which main step is being refined.

1 Get results

1.1 Open marks file
1.2 Start fixed loop for each pupil
1.3 Read pupil name into pupilName()
1.4 Read prelim mark into prelimMark()
1.5 Read course mark into courseMark()
1.6 End fixed loop
1.7 Close marks file

The main step says what the module does. The refinement explains how it does it.

You do not need to refine every main step. A step only needs refinement if it is complex or unclear.

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
The pseudocode below designs a program that reads pupil marks from a file, calculates percentages, finds the top pupil, and displays the result.

First, the top-level design and data flow are shown.

Pseudocode Data flow 1 Get results OUT: pupilName(), prelimMark(), courseMark() 2 Calculate percentages IN: prelimMark(), courseMark()OUT: percentage() 3 Find position of pupil with top mark IN: percentage()OUT: topPosition 4 Display pupil with top mark IN: pupilName(), percentage(), topPosition

Then, refinements are added for modules that need more detail.

1.1 Open marks file
1.2 Start fixed loop for each pupil
1.3 Read pupil name into pupilName()
1.4 Read prelim mark into prelimMark()
1.5 Read course mark into courseMark()
1.6 End fixed loop
1.7 Close marks file

2.1 Start fixed loop for each pupil
2.2 Set percentage() to (prelimMark() + courseMark()) / 1.5
2.3 End fixed loop

3.1 Set topPosition to first position
3.2 Start fixed loop from second pupil
3.3 If percentage() is greater than percentage(topPosition) then
3.4     Set topPosition to current position
3.5 End if
3.6 End fixed loop

4.1 Display pupilName(topPosition), percentage(topPosition)

This is detailed enough for a programmer to implement, but it is still a design rather than finished code.

docs.title: How Much Detail is Enough?
docs.text:
Pseudocode should be clear enough to implement, but it does not need exact programming language syntax.

Suitable design pseudocode:

3.3 If percentage() is greater than percentage(topPosition) then

Finished Python code:

if percentage[counter] > percentage[top_position]:

At the design stage, the first version is enough because it clearly explains the decision being made.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
Avoid these mistakes in Higher pseudocode:

  • writing vague steps such as Process data
  • missing IN and OUT data flow
  • refining a step with code that is too language-specific
  • adding refinements that do not match the main algorithm numbering
  • showing keyboard, screen, or file as data flow instead of variables or arrays

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Read the main algorithm below.

1 Load product data
2 Calculate total stock value
3 Find product with lowest stock
4 Display stock report

Step 3 could be refined as:

3.1 Set lowestPosition to first position
3.2 Start fixed loop from second product
3.3 If stockLevel() is less than stockLevel(lowestPosition) then
3.4     Set lowestPosition to current position
3.5 End if
3.6 End fixed loop

This refinement gives the logic for finding the lowest stock level without turning the design into full program code.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
Good Higher pseudocode should:

  • use clear module names
  • show IN and OUT data flow
  • number refinements to match the main algorithm
  • include important loops, decisions, and calculations
  • be detailed enough for a programmer to implement
  • avoid becoming full program code too early

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Pseudocode is a design technique used to describe an algorithm without using a specific programming language.

At Higher, pseudocode should show the top-level design, data flow, and refinements. It should make clear what each module does, what data it needs, and what data it produces.

A good Higher pseudocode design should help another programmer understand how the solution will work before implementation begins.

docs.title: Data Flow In and Out
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

You must be able to identify the data that flows into and out of modules in a design.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Data flow shows the information passed between modules in a program design.

At Higher, it is not enough to show that a program has modules. You also need to show what data each module needs and what data it produces.

This helps another programmer understand:

  • which modules depend on each other
  • what variables or arrays are passed between modules
  • what parameters may be needed when the program is implemented

docs.title: The Main Rule
docs.text:
Only show data flow when data moves between modules.

Do not list external sources or destinations as data flow.

Do not show Show instead Keyboard The variable that stores the input File The variables or arrays read from the file Screen The variables needed to produce the output Printed report The variables needed to create the report

For example, a module may read pupil marks from a file. The file is not shown as data flow. The arrays created from the file are shown as data flow because they are passed to other modules.

1 Get results
  OUT: pupilName(), prelimMark(), courseMark()

The module produces pupilName(), prelimMark(), and courseMark() for later modules to use.

docs.title: IN, OUT, and IN/OUT
docs.text:
Data flow is usually labelled using IN, OUT, or IN/OUT.

Direction Meaning Example IN Data passed into a module marks() OUT Data produced by a module and passed out average IN/OUT Data passed in, changed, and passed back out total

Use these questions to decide the direction:

  • Does the module need this data before it can work? Use IN.
  • Does the module create this data for another module to use? Use OUT.
  • Does the module receive the data, change it, and pass it back? Use IN/OUT.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
The top-level design below has three modules.

1 Get scores
2 Calculate average
3 Display average

To add data flow, think about what each module needs and produces.

docs.title: 1 Get scores
docs.text:
This module gets the scores from the user or from a file.

The keyboard or file is not shown as data flow because it is outside the module design.

1 Get scores
  OUT: score()

The module produces the score() array.

docs.title: 2 Calculate average
docs.text:
This module needs the scores before it can calculate the average.

2 Calculate average
  IN: score()
  OUT: average

The module receives score() and produces average.

docs.title: 3 Display average
docs.text:
This module needs the average so it can display it.

3 Display average
  IN: average

The screen is not shown as data flow. The module uses average to produce the screen output, but it does not pass new data to another module.

The complete data flow design is:

1 Get scores
  OUT: score()

2 Calculate average
  IN: score()
  OUT: average

3 Display average
  IN: average

docs.title: What Counts as Data Flow?
docs.text:
Ask this question:

Is this data being passed from one module to another module?

If the answer is yes, it is data flow. If the answer is no, it is probably an external input, external output, or data used only inside one module.

Action Is it data flow? Why? User types a mark No The data comes from outside the program design A module reads names from a file No The file is external to the module structure A module passes names() to another module Yes Data moves between modules A module calculates average for another module to display Yes The calculated value is passed to another module A module displays a result on screen No The result is sent outside the module design A module uses a counter inside a loop No The counter is only used inside that module

Common mistake

Do not list the keyboard, screen, or a file as data flow. Show the variables or arrays that move between modules.

docs.title: Data Flow in a Structure Diagram
docs.text:
Data flow can be shown on a structure diagram using labels or arrows.

If the diagram becomes crowded, the same information can be shown in a table.

A data flow table should list the module names and the data that moves in or out of each one.

For example:

Module IN OUT Get song data songName(), artistName(), downloads() Find most-downloaded song downloads() topPosition Display most-downloaded song songName(), artistName(), downloads(), topPosition

docs.title: Data Flow in Pseudocode
docs.text:
The same data flow can be shown beside the steps in pseudocode.

1 Get song data
  OUT: songName(), artistName(), downloads()

2 Find most-downloaded song
  IN: downloads()
  OUT: topPosition

3 Display most-downloaded song
  IN: songName(), artistName(), downloads(), topPosition

The brackets in names such as songName() and downloads() show that they are arrays.

docs.title: Link to Parameters
docs.text:
Data flow helps you decide the parameters for procedures and functions.

Find position of pupil with top mark
IN: percentage()
OUT: topPosition

This could become a function that receives percentage as a parameter and returns topPosition.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
A good data flow design should:

  • use meaningful data names
  • show arrays clearly, often using brackets such as marks()
  • show whether data is IN, OUT, or IN/OUT
  • avoid listing files, screens, keyboards, or reports as data flow
  • match the modules in the structure diagram or pseudocode
  • make the parameters for implementation clear

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Data flow shows the information passed between modules in a design.

The main rule is that data flow only shows data moving from one module to another. It should not show external sources or destinations such as the keyboard, screen, files, or printed reports.

A good Higher data flow design should show:

  • what data each module needs
  • what data each module produces
  • which variables or arrays move between modules
  • whether the data is IN, OUT, or IN/OUT
  • how the data flow could become parameters in the final program

Data flow helps another programmer understand how information moves through the solution before the program is implemented.

docs.title: Wireframes
docs.text:
What You Need to Know

You must be able to design user interfaces using wireframes.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
A wireframe is a simple design for a user interface.

It shows the layout of a screen before the final program is built. A wireframe is not meant to be a finished visual design. It should focus on what the user will see and how the user will interact with the program.

Wireframes help developers plan:

  • what information the user must enter
  • what buttons or controls the user will need
  • where outputs will be displayed
  • how the screen will support the functional requirements

docs.title: Wireframes and Analysis
docs.text:
A wireframe should be based on the analysis stage.

The analysis identifies the program's inputs, processes, and outputs. The wireframe should show how the user interface will support these.

Analysis item What the wireframe should show Input Where the user enters or selects data Process The button or control that starts an action Output Where the result or message will be displayed

For example, if the analysis says the user must enter two scores and view an average, the wireframe should include:

  • two score input boxes
  • a calculate button
  • an output area for the average

docs.title: What to Include
docs.text:
A good Higher wireframe may show:

  • headings
  • labels
  • input boxes
  • buttons
  • menus or drop-down lists
  • checkboxes or radio buttons
  • output areas
  • error or message areas
  • the general screen layout

The wireframe should make it clear how the user will complete the main tasks in the program.

docs.title: What Not to Worry About
docs.text:
A wireframe does not need to show the final appearance of the program.

You do not need to include:

  • colours
  • fonts
  • images
  • exact spacing
  • decorative styling

The main purpose is to show the layout and the interface elements, not the final graphic design.

docs.title: Example Wireframe
docs.text:
The example below shows a simple screen for entering quiz scores and displaying an average.

This wireframe shows:

  • where the user enters the pupil name and scores
  • the button used to start the calculation
  • where the average score will be displayed

docs.title: Checking a Wireframe
docs.text:
When checking a wireframe, ask:

  • Can the user enter all required inputs?
  • Can the user start the required processes?
  • Can the user see the required outputs?
  • Are labels clear enough for the user to understand?
  • Does the layout match the functional requirements?

If an input, process, or output from the analysis is missing, the wireframe is incomplete.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
A good Higher wireframe should:

  • show the main parts of the screen clearly
  • include all required inputs and outputs
  • include buttons or controls for important actions
  • use clear labels
  • match the functional requirements
  • be simple and easy to understand
  • avoid unnecessary decoration

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Wireframes are used to design the layout of a user interface before implementation begins.

At Higher, a wireframe should link clearly to the analysis. It should show how the user will enter data, start processes, and view outputs.

A good wireframe does not need to look like the finished program. It should clearly show the interface elements needed to meet the functional requirements.

docs.title: Design Tasks: Modules and Data Flow
docs.text:
Use each scenario to practise a different Higher design technique.

Each task tells you whether to present your answer as a:

  • structure diagram
  • pseudocode design
  • data flow table

Remember:

  • IN means data passed into a module
  • OUT means data passed out of a module
  • files, keyboards, screens and users are not data flow
  • data flow should show the variables or arrays passed between modules
Task Required design technique Task 1: Countries Structure diagram Task 2: Test Marks Data flow table Task 3: Aircraft Capacity Pseudocode design Task 4: Ticket Booking Structure diagram

docs.title: Task 1: Countries
docs.text:
Write a program that reads in a list of one hundred countries from a text file.

It asks the user to enter a capital letter and uses input validation to make sure only one character is entered.

Then it runs through every country in the list and checks if it starts with that letter. If so, it should add 1 to a counter.

At the end of the program, it displays the number of countries starting with that letter.

Required technique: Structure diagram

Create a structure diagram for this program. Show the modules and the data flow between them.

Use the module and data flow details below to help build your diagram.

Module IN OUT Read countries from text file Countries Get capital letter from user Letter Is only 1 character entered? Letter Valid Find country that meets criteria Countries, Letter Counter Display number of countries that meet criteria Counter

docs.title: Task 2: Test Marks
docs.text:
A teacher has a text file containing each pupil's name, and for each pupil, three test marks out of 20.

The program should read this data from a text file. The second module should use the data to calculate three grades, A, B and C, for each pupil: one for each test.

The next module should count how many pupils got three As, and the final module should display how many this was.

Required technique: Data flow table

Complete a data flow table for this program. Show the data that flows into and out of each module.

docs.title: Task 3: Aircraft Capacity
docs.text:
An airline uses a program to decide the most efficient aircraft to assign to a particular route.

There is a text file containing a list of aircraft types, their range, and passenger capacity.

The program needs to ask the user to input the number of passengers on a route, and the distance between airports.

The program should then loop through the aircraft types and find the smallest aircraft that can hold that many passengers while having enough range. It should then display the name of this aircraft type.

Required technique: Pseudocode design

Write the top-level pseudocode design for this program. Show the data flow on the right-hand side of each main step.

Use the module and data flow details below to help build your pseudocode.

Module IN OUT Read aircraft name, capacity and range from text file Names, Capacities, Ranges Get passenger number and range needed from user PassengerNum, RangeRequired Find smallest aircraft that meets these criteria Names, Capacities, Ranges, PassengerNum, RangeRequired SelectedName Display name of selected aircraft SelectedName

docs.title: Task 4: Ticket Booking
docs.text:
A ticket booking system allows users to go online to buy concert tickets.

It has a text file containing a list of current bookings. It gets user input for how many tickets they want to buy.

It checks how many tickets have already been booked in the file and calculates if there are still tickets available.

If there are tickets available, it passes the ticket cost to another module.

The program displays the cost. It then adds the new booking to the file.

Required technique: Structure diagram

Create a structure diagram for this program. Show the modules and the data flow between them.

Use the module and data flow details below to help build your diagram.

Module IN OUT Read text file with current bookings data Bookings Get number of required tickets from user TicketsWanted Are new tickets still available? Bookings, TicketsWanted Available, NewBooking Display total cost TicketCost TotalCost Write new booking into text file NewBooking

docs.title: Software Implementation
docs.text:
Higher course requirement

You must be able to describe, exemplify, implement, read and explain the structures, constructs and algorithms in this section using a procedural high-level language.

This section contains the implementation knowledge introduced or extended at Higher. It assumes that you can already use National 5 constructs such as variables, basic data types, selection, loops and ordinary 1D arrays.

docs.title: Suggested Learning Journey
docs.text:
Work through the lessons in this order. Each stage introduces ideas needed by the lessons that follow.

  1. Planning with sub-programs — divide a problem into modules and identify their names, inputs and outputs.
  2. Creating and calling sub-programs — implement procedures, functions, parameters and return values.
  3. Scope of variables — distinguish local and global variables and develop clear data flow.
  4. Putting it all together — progress from reading small examples to implementing complete modular programs.
  5. Pre-defined functions — use the required substring, character-code, integer-conversion and modulus operations.
  6. Parallel 1D arrays — connect related values using a shared index.
  7. Records — combine fields of different data types.
  8. Arrays of records — store and process several records.
  9. Records: putting it all together — apply records and arrays of records in one program.
  10. Sequential text files — create, read, write and close persistent text data.
  11. Sequential CSV files — process structured rows and fields.
  12. File handling: putting it all together — read, process and write file data in a modular program.
  13. Linear search — locate a target in a 1D array or array of records.
  14. Find minimum and maximum — track an extreme value while traversing a collection.
  15. Count occurrences — count values or records that satisfy a condition.
  16. Algorithms: putting it all together — combine the three standard algorithms in one problem.

The final Algorithms activity applies the structures, loops and indexing developed in the earlier lessons.

docs.title: What Is Prerequisite Knowledge?
docs.text: Input/output, assignment, arithmetic, string concatenation, Boolean logic, selection, fixed and conditional loops, and basic 1D-array traversal remain necessary programming knowledge. They are inherited from National 5 rather than new Higher implementation outcomes, so they are used throughout these pages instead of being repeated as separate Higher topics.

docs.title: Parallel 1D Arrays
docs.text:
What you need to know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement parallel 1D arrays.

docs.title: Related Data in Separate Arrays
docs.text:
A 1D array stores a collection of related values. In a set of parallel arrays, the value at one index is related to the values at the same index in the other arrays.

pupil_names = ["Peter", "Laura", "Marie"]
pupil_marks = [20, 21, 23]

The arrays are parallel because:

  • pupil_names[0] and pupil_marks[0] both describe Peter
  • pupil_names[1] and pupil_marks[1] both describe Laura
  • pupil_names[2] and pupil_marks[2] both describe Marie

The index connects the related values.

Index pupil_names pupil_marks 0 Peter 20 1 Laura 21 2 Marie 23

docs.title: Accessing Corresponding Values
docs.text:
Use the same index with every parallel array:

pupil_names = ["Peter", "Laura", "Marie"]
pupil_marks = [20, 21, 23]

index = 2
print(pupil_names[index], "scored", pupil_marks[index])

This displays Marie's name and mark. Using different indexes would combine values belonging to different pupils.

docs.title: Traversing Parallel Arrays
docs.text:
A loop can process every pupil while keeping the arrays aligned:

pupil_names = ["Peter", "Laura", "Marie"]
pupil_marks = [20, 21, 23]

for index in range(len(pupil_names)):
    print(pupil_names[index], "scored", pupil_marks[index])

The arrays should contain the same number of elements. The program uses the length of one array because matching elements occupy matching positions.

docs.title: Adding Related Data
docs.text:
When adding a new item, update every parallel array:

pupil_names = []
pupil_marks = []

name = input("Enter pupil name: ")
mark = int(input("Enter pupil mark: "))

pupil_names.append(name)
pupil_marks.append(mark)

Both values are added at the same index, so their relationship is preserved.

docs.title: Updating Corresponding Values
docs.text:
Use the same index when changing a value in one of the arrays:

pupil_names = ["Peter", "Laura", "Marie"]
pupil_marks = [20, 21, 23]

pupil_marks[1] = 24
print(pupil_names[1], "scored", pupil_marks[1])

Index 1 represents Laura in both arrays, so the program changes Laura's mark and displays Laura scored 24.

docs.title: Strengths and Risks
docs.text:
Parallel arrays are straightforward when a problem already uses 1D arrays, but their indexes must remain synchronised. Adding, removing or sorting a value in one array without making the same change to the others breaks the relationship.

Records provide another way to group related values. They are introduced in the next lesson.

Check Your Understanding

A shop needs a program that displays the name and price of each product. The main program is shown below, but the two parallel arrays have not yet been created.

for index in range(len(product_names)):
    print(product_names[index], "£", product_prices[index])

Create and test the completed program in Python. Take a screenshot showing your code and its output, then paste it into your workbook.

You should:

  1. write product_names above the main program and store Notebook, Pen, Folder and Pencil
  2. write product_prices as a parallel array and store 2.50, 1.20, 3.00 and 0.80
  3. make sure each price has the same index as its product
  4. identify the values stored at index 2 in both arrays
  5. explain why the program uses the same index with both arrays

Use the following table to test your program:

Index Product name Product price Expected output 0 Notebook 2.50 Notebook £ 2.5 1 Pen 1.20 Pen £ 1.2 2 Folder 3.00 Folder £ 3.0 3 Pencil 0.80 Pencil £ 0.8

docs.title: Planning with Sub-programs
docs.text:
What you need to know

You must be able to explain why programs are divided into sub-programs and identify each sub-program by its name, inputs and outputs.

A sub-program is a named section of a program that performs one clear task. Breaking a large problem into smaller sub-programs is called modular design.

docs.title: Why Use Sub-programs?
docs.text:
Sub-programs can make a program:

  • easier to understand because each part has one purpose
  • easier to test because each part can be checked separately
  • easier to maintain because a change can be made in one place
  • easier to reuse because the same sub-program can be called more than once
  • easier to develop as a team because different programmers can work on different modules

docs.title: From a Problem to Modules
docs.text:
Consider a program that calculates and displays a pupil's percentage. It can be divided into three stages:

1. Get the pupil's details and marks
2. Calculate the percentage
3. Display the result

This is a top-level design. Each line describes a module without yet showing the detailed algorithm.

Good module names begin with a verb and clearly describe the task:

Unclear name Clearer name details get_pupil_details percentage calculate_percentage screen display_result

docs.title: Inputs and Outputs
docs.text:
Before implementing a module, identify the data that crosses its boundary:

  • an input is data the module needs
  • an output is data the module produces for another part of the program
Calculate percentage
IN: mark, total
OUT: percentage

The calculation also creates temporary values, but only data that crosses the module boundary is listed as an input or output.

docs.title: Procedures and Functions
docs.text:
There are two kinds of sub-program at Higher:

  • A procedure performs an action. For example, it might display a result.
  • A function calculates and returns a value to the caller.

At this stage, concentrate on each module's purpose and data flow. The next lesson shows how procedures, functions, parameters and return values are implemented in Python.

Check Your Understanding

A program asks for the length and width of a room, calculates its area and displays the answer.

In your workbook:

  1. write a three-step top-level design
  2. give each module a meaningful name
  3. identify the inputs and outputs of each module

docs.title: Creating and Calling Sub-programs
docs.text:
What you need to know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement procedures, functions, parameter passing, and formal and actual parameters.

The main program controls the solution by calling sub-programs in the required order.

docs.title: A Procedure Without Parameters
docs.text:
Start with a procedure that performs one action:

def display_heading():
    print("Pupil Results")

display_heading()

def defines the procedure. The final line calls it. Program execution moves into the procedure and returns to the main program when the procedure ends.

docs.title: Passing Data into a Procedure
docs.text:
Most sub-programs need data from the caller. A parameter allows that data to be passed in.

def display_result(name, score):
    print(name, "scored", score)

pupil_name = "Aisha"
pupil_score = 84
display_result(pupil_name, pupil_score)

The values flow from the main program into the procedure:

display_result(pupil_name, pupil_score)
                    |             |
                    v             v
     def display_result(name, score):

docs.title: Formal and Actual Parameters
docs.text:
Term Example Meaning Formal parameter name, score Placeholder in the sub-program definition Actual parameter (argument) pupil_name, pupil_score Value or variable supplied in the call

The first actual parameter is passed to the first formal parameter, the second to the second, and so on. Their order therefore matters.

docs.title: Returning Data from a Function
docs.text:
A function sends a result back with return:

def calculate_percentage(mark, total):
    percentage = mark / total * 100
    return percentage

pupil_percentage = calculate_percentage(42, 50)
print("Percentage:", pupil_percentage)

mark and total are inputs. percentage is the output. The returned value is stored in pupil_percentage in the main program.

docs.title: Procedure or Function?
docs.text:
Feature Procedure Function Performs a task Yes Yes Can receive parameters Yes Yes Returns a result to the caller No Yes Typical call display_result(name, score) result = calculate_total(price, quantity)

Use a function when another part of the program needs the calculated value. Use a procedure when the sub-program only needs to perform an action.

docs.title: A Complete Modular Program
docs.text:
def get_mark():
    mark = int(input("Enter the mark: "))
    return mark

def calculate_percentage(mark, total):
    percentage = mark / total * 100
    return percentage

def display_percentage(percentage):
    print("Percentage:", percentage)

pupil_mark = get_mark()
pupil_percentage = calculate_percentage(pupil_mark, 50)
display_percentage(pupil_percentage)

Read the final three lines first to see the overall flow. The sub-program definitions contain the detail for each stage.

Exam language

Formal parameters appear in the definition. Actual parameters appear in the call. Inputs normally enter through parameters and outputs normally leave through return.

Check Your Understanding

A decorator needs a program that calculates the floor area of a rectangular room. The room's length and width are measured in metres. The main program is shown below, but the calculate_area function has not yet been written.

room_length = 4.5
room_width = 3.0
area = calculate_area(room_length, room_width)
print("Floor area:", area, "square metres")

Create and test the completed program in Python. Take a screenshot showing your code and its output, then paste it into your workbook.

You should:

  1. write calculate_area above the main program
  2. give the function two formal parameters
  3. calculate and return the room's area
  4. identify the actual parameters used in the function call
  5. identify the function's inputs and output

Use the following table to test your program:

Length Width Expected area Expected output 4.5 3.0 13.5 Floor area: 13.5 square metres

docs.title: Scope of Variables
docs.text:
What you need to know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement the scope of local and global variables.

The scope of a variable is the part of a program where it can be accessed. Understanding scope helps you decide what data must be passed between the main program and its sub-programs.

docs.title: Local Variables
docs.text:
A local variable belongs to one sub-program and can only be accessed there. Formal parameters are also local to their sub-program.

def calculate_total(price, quantity):
    total = price * quantity
    return total

order_total = calculate_total(3.50, 4)
print(order_total)

Inside calculate_total, the variables price, quantity and total are local. The main program cannot access them directly. order_total receives the function's output and belongs to the main program.

docs.title: Global Variables
docs.text:
A global variable is created outside every sub-program.

vat_rate = 0.20

def add_vat(price):
    final_price = price * (1 + vat_rate)
    return final_price

vat_rate is global, so add_vat can read it. The formal parameter price and the variable final_price are local.

docs.title: Prefer Clear Data Flow
docs.text:
Passing required data as parameters usually makes a sub-program easier to understand, test and reuse:

    return final_price

This version states both inputs in the definition and call. It does not depend on a hidden global value.

docs.title: Same Name, Different Variable
docs.text: A local variable can have the same name as a global variable. They are separate variables, and the local version hides the global one inside that sub-program. Using distinct, meaningful names usually avoids confusion.

docs.title: Pre-defined Functions
docs.text:
What you need to know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement pre-defined functions with parameters to create substrings, convert characters to character codes and back, convert floating-point values to integers, and calculate modulus.

A pre-defined function is supplied by the programming language. It can be called without writing its algorithm yourself.

docs.title: Substrings
docs.text:
A substring is part of a string. Python slicing uses a start index that is included and an end index that is excluded.

message = "Higher Computing"
course = message[0:6]
subject = message[7:16]

course becomes "Higher" and subject becomes "Computing".

docs.title: Character Codes
docs.text:
Python's ord() converts one character to its Unicode code point; chr() performs the reverse operation. For ordinary ASCII characters, these values match their ASCII codes.

code = ord("A")       # 65
character = chr(66)  # "B"

docs.title: Floating Point to Integer
docs.text:
int() converts a floating-point value to an integer by discarding the fractional part (truncating towards zero). This is not rounding.

positive = int(7.9)   # 7
negative = int(-7.9)  # -7

docs.title: Modulus
docs.text:
The modulus operator % returns the remainder after integer division.

remainder = 17 % 5  # 2

if number % 2 == 0:
    print("Even")

Common uses include checking whether a number is even, wrapping a counter, and testing divisibility.

docs.text:
What you need to know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement a linear search using a 1D array or an array of records.

A linear search checks each element in order until the whole array has been searched. It can record whether a target exists or the position where it was found.

docs.title: Recording Whether a Target Was Found
docs.text:
names = ["Aisha", "Lewis", "Maya", "Callum"]
target = input("Enter a name: ")
found = False

for index in range(len(names)):
    if names[index] == target:
        found = True

print("Name found:", found)

The Boolean begins as False and only changes when an element matches the target.

docs.title: Recording the Position
docs.text:
position = -1

for index in range(len(names)):
    if names[index] == target:
        position = index

-1 is used because it cannot be a valid array index. If it remains -1, the target was not found.

Check before using the position

Do not use array[position] until you have checked that position is not -1.

docs.title: Search Checklist
docs.text:
1. Set found to False or position to -1.
  2. Traverse the array.
  3. Compare each element with the target.
  4. Update found or position when a match occurs.

docs.title: Counting Exact Matches

marks = [72, 41, 88, 50, 36, 61]
pass_count = 0

for index in range(len(marks)):
    if marks[index] >= 50:
        pass_count = pass_count + 1

Count or total?

A count adds 1 for each match. A running total adds the value itself.

docs.text:
What you need to know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement opening, creating, reading, writing and closing sequential text files.

A file keeps data after a program stops. A sequential file is processed in order, from the beginning to the end.

docs.title: File Modes
docs.text: Mode Purpose Important effect "r" Read The file must already exist. "w" Create and write Existing contents are replaced. "a" Append New data is added at the end.

docs.title: Creating and Writing
docs.text:
file = open("scores.txt", "w")
file.write("55\n")
file.write("72\n")
file.write("64\n")
file.close()

Opening with "w" creates scores.txt if required. \n starts a new line. The file is closed after the program finishes using it.

Write mode

Opening an existing file with "w" removes its previous contents.

docs.title: Reading a Whole File
docs.text:
file = open("scores.txt", "r")
contents = file.read()
file.close()
print(contents)

docs.title: Reading One Line at a Time
docs.text:
file = open("scores.txt", "r")

for line in file:
    score = int(line.strip())
    print(score)

file.close()

strip() removes the newline character and int() converts the text into an integer.

for row in reader:
    name = row[0]
    age = int(row[1])
    registration_class = row[2]

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
What you need to know

You must be able to describe, exemplify and implement records.

A record groups related fields that may have different data types. A pupil record could contain a string name, an integer age and a Boolean permission.

docs.title: Defining a Record
docs.text:
Python can represent a record with a dataclass:

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Pupil:
    name: str = ""
    age: int = 0
    permission: bool = False

Pupil is the record structure. name, age and permission are its fields. Each field has an identifier, a data type and a default value.

docs.title: Creating and Updating a Record
docs.text:
pupil = Pupil()
pupil.name = "Aisha"
pupil.age = 16
pupil.permission = True

pupil is one record created from the Pupil structure. Dot notation selects a field, such as pupil.name.

Values can also be supplied when the record is created:

pupil = Pupil("Aisha", 16, True)

docs.title: Reading Fields
docs.text:
print("Name:", pupil.name)
print("Age:", pupil.age)
print("Permission:", pupil.permission)

Records keep all the data about one item together. This is clearer than using separate, unrelated variables such as pupil_name, pupil_age and pupil_permission.

What you need to know

An array of records stores several records with the same structure. Each element represents one complete item.

docs.title: Creating an Array of Records
docs.text:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Pupil:
    name: str = ""
    age: int = 0
    registration_class: str = ""

pupils = [Pupil() for index in range(3)]

pupils contains three empty Pupil records. A field is selected using an array index followed by dot notation, such as pupils[0].name.

docs.title: Entering Data
docs.text:

    pupils[index].name = input("Enter name: ")
    pupils[index].age = int(input("Enter age: "))
    pupils[index].registration_class = input("Enter registration class: ")

The same index is used for all fields belonging to one pupil.

docs.title: Traversing the Array
docs.text:

    print(pupils[index].name, pupils[index].age,
          pupils[index].registration_class)

The loop visits every record in order. Unlike parallel arrays, each pupil's related values stay together inside one element.

for index in range(len(pupils)):

docs.title: Storing Negative Numbers (Two's Complement)
docs.text:
What you need to Know

Describe and exemplify the use of binary to represent positive and negative integers using two’s complement, including the range of numbers that can be represented using a fixed number of bits.

docs.title: Sign bits
docs.text:
The first bit in a binary number is called the sign bit. It is the bit furthest to the left.

In two's complement:

  • a sign bit of 0 means the number is positive
  • a sign bit of 1 means the number is negative

The method for representing negative numbers is called two's complement.

docs.title: Creating a negative number
docs.text:
To store a negative number, computers use a method called two's complement.

To create a negative number using two's complement, use this method:

  1. Write out the positive version of the number.
  2. Flip all the bits.
  3. Add 1.

This is often remembered as:

Think positive → Flip the bits → Add 1

Remember

To create a negative number:

Think Positive → Flip the Bits → Add 1

Example 1

Find the binary number for -75.

First, write out +75.

+75 = 64 + 8 + 2 + 1

Step Binary Think positive 0100 1011 Flip the bits 1011 0100 Add 1 1011 0101

The Add 1 row is found by adding 0000 0001 to the flipped bits:

Step Binary Flipped bits 1011 0100 Add 1 0000 0001 Result 1011 0101

In this example, the flipped bits end in 0, so adding 1 changes the last bit to 1. There is no carry.

So -75 is stored as:

1011 0101

Example 2

Find the binary number for -28.

First, write out +28.

+28 = 16 + 8 + 4

Step Binary Think positive 0001 1100 Flip the bits 1110 0011 Add 1 1110 0100

The Add 1 row is found by adding 0000 0001 to the flipped bits:

Step Binary Flipped bits 1110 0011 Add 1 0000 0001 Result 1110 0100

In this example, the flipped bits end in 11. Adding 1 changes those ending 1==s to ==0==s until the first ==0 becomes 1.

So -28 is stored as:

1110 0100

docs.title: Step 1: Look at the first bit
docs.text: First Bit Meaning 0 Positive number 1 Negative number

docs.title: If the first bit is 0
docs.text:
Convert the number to denary as normal.

Example:

0100 1011

64 + 8 + 2 + 1 = 75

docs.title: If the first bit is 1
docs.text:
Use the following method:

  1. Flip all the bits
  2. Add 1
  3. Convert to denary
  4. Add a minus sign

Example

Read 1110 0100

Step Result Original number 1110 0100 Flip the bits 0001 1011 Add 1 0001 1100 Convert to denary 16 + 8 + 4 = 28 Add minus sign -28

Therefore:

1110 0100 = -28

Exam Tip

Always check the first bit before doing anything else.

  • 0 = Positive
  • 1 = Negative

docs.title: 8-bit Two's Complement Range
docs.text:
-128 to 127

You should know this range for Higher Computing Science.

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
An 8-bit number has 256 possible combinations.

Because two's complement stores both positive and negative numbers:

  • Half are used for negative numbers.
  • Half are used for positive numbers and zero.
Smallest Value Largest Value -128 127

docs.title: Easy Way to Remember
docs.text:
For an n-bit two's complement number:

Range = -2^(n-1) to (2^(n-1) - 1)

For 8 bits:

  • Smallest value = -2^7 = -128
  • Largest value = 2^7 - 1 = 127

Exam Tip

Many pupils incorrectly write:

-127 to 127

The correct range is:

-128 to 127

There is always one more negative number than positive number.
