docs.title: Representing Floating-Point Numbers
docs.text:
What you need to know

Describe and exemplify how positive and negative real numbers are stored using a mantissa and an exponent.

Describe how the number of bits allocated to the mantissa and exponent affects precision and range.

docs.title: Why floating point is used
docs.text:
An integer is a whole number, such as 25 or -8. A real number can contain a fractional part, such as 4.75 or 0.001.

Computers use floating-point representation to store very large, very small and fractional real numbers. It works like scientific notation, but uses powers of 2 instead of powers of 10.

For example, the binary number 100.01 can be written as:

0.10001 × 23

This means:

  • 0.10001 stores the significant bits of the number
  • 23 shows that the binary point has moved 3 places

In floating-point representation, the value is split into two parts:

Part Purpose Mantissa Stores the significant bits of the number and its sign Exponent Stores how far the binary point has moved

The binary point

A binary point works like a decimal point, but it separates whole and fractional binary place values.

docs.title: The mantissa, exponent and normalisation
docs.text:
At Higher, the mantissa and exponent are stored slightly differently.

The mantissa uses a sign bit:

  • 0 for a positive number
  • 1 for a negative number

The exponent is stored using two's complement, so it can represent positive and negative movements of the binary point.

Before a number is stored, move the binary point so that the mantissa begins .1. This is called normalising the number.

The sign bit and the exponent answer different questions. Do not mix them up.

To decide the mantissa sign bit Result No minus sign Use 0 at the start of the mantissa Minus sign Use 1 at the start of the mantissa To decide the exponent Result Number is bigger than 1, so the binary point moves left Positive exponent Number is smaller than 1, so the binary point moves right Negative exponent

Normalising and reading back

When you are normalising the original number, moving the binary point right gives a negative exponent.

When you are reading the stored number back, a negative exponent moves the binary point left again.

This is because reading it back reverses the normalising step.

Example 1: binary point moves left

Convert the positive number 100.001101 using a 16-bit mantissa and an 8-bit exponent.

The first 1 in 100.001101 is part of the original number. It is not the mantissa sign bit yet.

Step 1: Normalise the number

As it is a positive number, normalise it so the mantissa begins .1.

Move the binary point 3 places left:

100.001101 becomes .100001101 × 23

You now add a 0 to show it is positive.

.100001101 becomes 0.100001101

As the binary point moved 3 places to the left, the exponent is therefore +3.

0.100001101 × 23

Step 2: Store the mantissa

Add zeros on the right until the mantissa contains 16 bits:

0.100001101000000

The binary point is not stored, so the stored mantissa is the remaining bits with a 0 at the start because it is a positive number:

0100 0011 0100 0000

Step 3: Store the exponent

Write +3 in 8-bit binary:

0000 0011

Mantissa Exponent 0100 0011 0100 0000 0000 0011

docs.title: Reading the stored mantissa
docs.text:
Once the mantissa has been stored, the binary point is not stored as one of the bits.

It is assumed because its position is always known. This saves space because the computer only needs to store the bits, not the point itself.

When reading the stored mantissa back, place the binary point between the first bit and the second bit.

This is only the fixed reading position for the stored mantissa. It is not the same as moving the original binary point left or right when normalising.

For example, the stored mantissa from Example 1 is:

0100 0011 0100 0000

This can be split up as:

First bit Assumed binary point Remaining bits 0 . 100001101000000

So it is read as:

0.100001101000000

Example 2: positive number less than 1

Convert the positive number 0.001010101 using a 16-bit mantissa and an 8-bit exponent.

This number is positive because there is no minus sign. It is less than 1 because it starts with 0..

This is like a denary number such as 0.8: it is positive, but it is still less than 1.

The exponent will be negative because the binary point needs to move right to normalise the number.

Step 1: Normalise the number

As it is a positive number, normalise it so the mantissa begins .1.

Move the binary point 2 places right:

0.001010101 becomes .1010101 × 2-2

You now add a 0 to show it is positive.

.1010101 becomes 0.1010101

The number is still positive, but the exponent is -2 because the binary point moved 2 places to the right.

0.1010101 × 2-2

Step 2: Store the mantissa

Add zeros on the right until the mantissa contains 16 bits:

0.101010100000000

The binary point is not stored, so the stored mantissa is the remaining bits with a 0 at the start because it is a positive number:

0101 0101 0000 0000

Step 3: Store the exponent

Store -2 as 8-bit two's complement:

1111 1110

Mantissa Exponent 0101 0101 0000 0000 1111 1110

docs.title: Representing a negative number
docs.text:
For a negative value, first normalise the positive magnitude. Then put a 1 sign bit at the start of the mantissa to show that the number is negative.

Common misconception

The mantissa is not converted using two's complement at Higher.

The exponent is stored using two's complement. The mantissa uses a sign bit.

Example 3: negative number

Convert -1000.00001 using a 16-bit mantissa and an 8-bit exponent.

This number is negative, but its size is bigger than 1.

The binary point will move left because of the size of the number.

The negative sign is shown separately using the mantissa sign bit.

Step 1: Normalise the positive magnitude

Ignore the minus sign temporarily and normalise the positive magnitude so the mantissa begins .1.

Move the binary point 4 places left:

1000.00001 becomes .100000001 × 24

The original number was negative, so put a 1 at the start of the mantissa to show it is negative.

As the binary point moved 4 places to the left, the exponent is therefore +4.

The normalised magnitude is:

.100000001 × 24

The stored mantissa will start with 1 because the original number was negative.

Step 2: Store the mantissa

Add zeros on the right until the mantissa contains 16 bits:

1.100000001000000

The binary point is not stored, so the stored mantissa is the remaining bits with a 1 at the start because it is a negative number:

1100 0000 0100 0000

Step 3: Store the exponent

Write +4 in 8-bit binary:

0000 0100

Mantissa Exponent 1100 0000 0100 0000 0000 0100

docs.title: More worked examples
docs.text:
The same method works for whole numbers, fractions and negative values. Always normalise first, then store the mantissa and exponent.

Example 4: positive mixed number

Convert the positive number 1.01 using a 16-bit mantissa and an 8-bit exponent.

The first 1 in 1.01 is part of the original number. It is not the mantissa sign bit yet.

Step 1: Normalise the number

As it is a positive number, normalise it so the mantissa begins .1.

Move the binary point 1 place left:

1.01 becomes .101 × 21

You now add a 0 to show it is positive.

.101 becomes 0.101

As the binary point moved 1 place to the left, the exponent is therefore +1.

0.101 × 21

Step 2: Store the mantissa

Add zeros on the right until the mantissa contains 16 bits:

0.101000000000000

The binary point is not stored, so the stored mantissa is the remaining bits with a 0 at the start because it is a positive number:

0101 0000 0000 0000

Step 3: Store the exponent

Write +1 in 8-bit binary:

0000 0001

Mantissa Exponent 0101 0000 0000 0000 0000 0001

Example 5: small positive fraction

Convert the positive number 0.0001101 using a 16-bit mantissa and an 8-bit exponent.

Step 1: Normalise the number

As it is a positive number, normalise it so the mantissa begins .1.

Move the binary point 3 places right:

0.0001101 becomes .1101 × 2-3

You now add a 0 to show it is positive.

.1101 becomes 0.1101

As the binary point moved 3 places to the right, the exponent is therefore -3.

0.1101 × 2-3

Step 2: Store the mantissa

Add zeros on the right until the mantissa contains 16 bits, including the sign bit:

0.110100000000000

The binary point is not stored, so the stored mantissa is the remaining bits with a 0 at the start because it is a positive number:

0110 1000 0000 0000

Step 3: Store the exponent

Write -3 as 8-bit two's complement:

Step Exponent +3 0000 0011 Flip all bits 1111 1100 Add 1 1111 1101 Mantissa Exponent 0110 1000 0000 0000 1111 1101

Example 6: negative fraction

Convert -0.01101 using a 16-bit mantissa and an 8-bit exponent.

Step 1: Normalise the positive magnitude

Ignore the minus sign temporarily and normalise the positive magnitude so the mantissa begins .1.

Move the binary point 1 place right:

0.01101 becomes .1101 × 2-1

The original number was negative, so put a 1 at the start of the mantissa to show it is negative.

As the binary point moved 1 place to the right, the exponent is therefore -1.

The normalised magnitude is:

.1101 × 2-1

The stored mantissa will start with 1 because the original number was negative.

Step 2: Store the mantissa

Add zeros on the right until the mantissa contains 16 bits, including the sign bit:

1.110100000000000

The binary point is not stored, so the stored mantissa is the remaining bits with a 1 at the start because it is a negative number:

1110 1000 0000 0000

Step 3: Store the exponent

Store -1 as 8-bit two's complement:

1111 1111

Mantissa Exponent 1110 1000 0000 0000 1111 1111

Example 7: reading a stored floating-point number

A number is stored using:

Mantissa Exponent 0100 1100 0000 0000 0000 0010

The mantissa is positive because it begins with 0.

Put the assumed binary point between the first bit and the second bit:

0.100110000000000

The exponent is 0000 0010, which is +2.

Move the binary point 2 places right:

0.100110000000000 × 22 = 10.011

So the stored value is:

10.011

docs.title: A method to remember
docs.text:
1. Ignore the minus sign temporarily and normalise the positive magnitude to begin .1.
  2. Count how many places the binary point moved.
  3. Add the sign bit at the start of the mantissa: 0 for positive, 1 for negative.
  4. Pad the mantissa on the right to the required length.
  5. Store the movement as the exponent. If the exponent is negative, use two's complement.

Exam tip

Keep the mantissa and exponent separate, and check their bit lengths before giving your final answer.

docs.title: Range and precision
docs.text: A fixed number of bits is shared between the mantissa and the exponent.

docs.title: Range
docs.text:
Range means the spread between the smallest and largest magnitudes that can be represented.

The exponent controls range because it controls how far the binary point can move.

  • More exponent bits give a greater range.
  • Fewer exponent bits give a smaller range.

docs.title: Precision
docs.text:
Precision means how accurately a value can be represented.

The mantissa controls precision because it stores the significant bits of the value.

  • More mantissa bits give greater precision.
  • Fewer mantissa bits give less precision, so more rounding may be required.

Precision example

Imagine that only four significant mantissa bits are available.

The value 0.1011011 cannot be stored exactly because it contains too many significant bits. Some bits must be removed and the stored value must be rounded.

With more mantissa bits, more of the original value could be kept.

Change Effect Increase exponent bits Increase range Decrease exponent bits Decrease range Increase mantissa bits Increase precision Decrease mantissa bits Decrease precision

Do not mix these up

Exponent = range

Mantissa = precision

If the total number of bits is fixed, giving more bits to one part leaves fewer bits for the other. This creates a trade-off between range and precision.

docs.title: Computer Architecture
docs.text:
What you need to know

Describe the purpose of the processor, memory, storage, input and output devices.

Describe the role of the control unit, arithmetic and logic unit, registers, cache and system buses.

Computer architecture describes the components of a computer system and how they work together to run programs.

Computers come in many forms, but they all follow the same basic pattern:

  1. Input enters the system.
  2. The processor works on the data by following instructions.
  3. Memory holds the programs and data currently being used.
  4. Storage keeps programs and data for later.
  5. Output presents the result.

For example, when you edit a photo, the image may be loaded from storage into memory. The processor follows the photo-editing program's instructions to change the image, and the updated image is shown on the screen as output.

docs.title: Input and output
docs.text:
Data can move into a computer system, out of a computer system, or both. This depends on the type of device being used.

InputOutputBothComparison

An input device sends data or instructions into a computer system.

Examples include:

  • a keyboard sending key presses;
  • a microphone sending sound data;
  • a camera sending image or video data; and
  • a mouse sending movement and click data.

An output device presents processed data from a computer system.

Examples include:

  • a monitor displaying text, images and video;
  • a speaker playing sound; and
  • a printer producing a physical copy.

Some devices perform both roles.

For example, a touchscreen is an output device because it displays images and text. It is also an input device because it detects taps, swipes and gestures.

A network interface also performs both roles because it sends and receives data.

The key difference is the direction of data flow:

Device type Direction Example Input Into the computer Typing a password on a keyboard Output Out of the computer Showing a message on a monitor

docs.title: The processor
docs.text:
The central processing unit (CPU) is the part of the computer that executes program instructions and controls the computer's operation.

The processor does not normally store whole programs permanently. Instead, it works on small pieces of data and instructions at very high speed.

In simple terms, the processor:

  1. gets an instruction from memory;
  2. works out what the instruction means;
  3. carries out the instruction; and
  4. moves on to the next instruction.

It contains several important components.

Control unitALURegistersPC and IRSummary

The control unit (CU) coordinates the processor's activities.

It decodes instructions and sends control signals to other components. It does not usually perform calculations itself. Its job is to direct the other parts of the processor.

For example, the control unit can signal that data should be read from memory, copied into a register, or sent to the ALU.

The arithmetic and logic unit (ALU) performs calculations, comparisons and logical operations.

Arithmetic operations include:

  • addition;
  • subtraction;
  • multiplication; and
  • division.

Logical operations include:

  • comparing two values;
  • checking whether a condition is true or false; and
  • using logic operations such as AND, OR and NOT.

For example, if a program checks whether a user's score is greater than 50, the comparison is carried out by the ALU.

Registers are very small, very fast storage locations inside the processor. They hold the values the processor needs immediately.

Registers are faster than cache, RAM and secondary storage, but there are only a small number of them.

Why registers matter

The processor cannot work directly on every item in RAM at once. Registers hold the current instruction, address or data value so the processor can use it immediately.

Different registers have specific jobs:

Register Purpose Program counter (PC) Stores the address of the next instruction to fetch from memory. Instruction register (IR) Stores the instruction currently being decoded or executed. Component Purpose Control unit (CU) Coordinates the processor's activities. It decodes instructions and sends control signals to other components. Arithmetic and logic unit (ALU) Performs calculations, comparisons and logical operations. Registers Very small, fast storage locations inside the processor that hold current instructions, addresses and data.

docs.title: Memory and storage
docs.text:
Memory and storage both hold programs and data, but they are used for different purposes.

Main memory stores the programs and data that the processor needs to access directly. Secondary storage keeps programs and data when the power is switched off.

RAMROMSecondary storageComparisonOpening a file

Random access memory (RAM) is the computer's working memory. It stores the programs and data currently being used.

When a program is running, its instructions and current data are held in RAM. The processor can then fetch instructions and data from memory as needed.

For example, when you open a web browser, the browser program is loaded into RAM. The web pages, images and tabs you are using are also stored in RAM while they are needed.

RAM is volatile, which means its contents are lost when the power is switched off.

Read-only memory (ROM) stores instructions or data that should not be lost when the computer is switched off. It is non-volatile.

ROM is often used to store firmware: permanent instructions used to start the computer and prepare it to load the operating system.

Secondary storage keeps programs and data when the power is switched off.

Examples include:

  • solid-state drives;
  • hard disk drives; and
  • memory cards.

Storage has a much larger capacity than RAM and is non-volatile, but the processor cannot execute instructions directly from it. A program must first be loaded from storage into RAM.

Feature Main memory Secondary storage Main purpose Holds programs and data currently in use Keeps programs and data for later Speed Faster Slower Capacity Smaller Larger Volatility RAM is volatile; ROM is non-volatile Non-volatile Example Open apps and current files Saved documents, installed apps and the operating system

Memory speed

RAM is normally much faster than secondary storage, but it is still slower than registers and cache.

When you open a saved document, it is read from secondary storage and copied into RAM.

The processor then works with the copy in RAM while the document is open. When you save the document, the updated version is written back to secondary storage.

docs.title: System buses
docs.text:
A bus is a collection of parallel lines used to carry signals between components.

Buses connect the processor, memory and input/output devices. They allow addresses, data and control signals to move around the computer system.

Address busData busControl busExample transferSummary

The address bus carries the address of the memory location or input/output port being accessed.

It normally carries addresses from the processor to other components.

The address bus identifies where a transfer should happen.

The data bus carries data and instructions.

It is bidirectional, which means data can travel to or from the processor.

The data bus carries what is being transferred.

The control bus carries control signals, such as read, write and timing signals.

It is bidirectional, which means signals travel between the processor and other components.

The control bus tells the other components what kind of action should happen.

To read an instruction from memory:

  1. The processor places the memory address on the address bus.
  2. The processor sends a read signal on the control bus.
  3. The instruction stored at that address travels back to the processor on the data bus.
Bus Purpose Direction Address bus Carries the address of the memory location or input/output port being accessed. Normally from the processor to other components. Data bus Carries data and instructions. Bidirectional: data can travel to or from the processor. Control bus Carries control signals such as read, write and timing signals. Bidirectional: signals travel between the processor and other components.

The three buses work together. The address bus alone is not enough because it only identifies a location. The data bus alone is not enough because the system also needs to know where the data is coming from or going to.

docs.title: Cache memory
docs.text:
Cache (pronounced cash) is a small amount of very fast memory located in or close to the processor. It stores copies of frequently or recently used instructions and data, reducing the time the processor spends waiting for RAM.

Cache is useful because processors are much faster than RAM. Without cache, the processor may spend more time waiting for data and instructions to arrive from memory.

PurposeHow it worksExample

Cache stores copies of frequently or recently used instructions and data.

This reduces the time the processor spends waiting for RAM.

When the processor needs data or an instruction:

  1. It checks cache first.
  2. If the item is in cache, it can be accessed quickly.
  3. If the item is not in cache, it must be fetched from RAM.

If a program repeats the same calculation many times, the same instructions may be needed again and again.

Cache can keep copies of those instructions close to the processor, so they can be fetched more quickly.

Cache is explored in more detail in Factors Affecting System Performance.

docs.title: How the parts work together
docs.text:
The components in a computer system do not work separately. They cooperate every time a program runs.

For example, when a user opens an app:

  1. The app is loaded from secondary storage into RAM.
  2. The processor fetches instructions from RAM.
  3. The control unit coordinates each instruction.
  4. The ALU performs any required calculations or comparisons.
  5. Registers hold the current instructions, addresses and data being used immediately.
  6. Cache stores copies of frequently used instructions and data to reduce waiting time.
  7. The buses carry addresses, data and control signals between components.
  8. Output devices present the result to the user.

Exam focus

For this topic, make sure you can describe the purpose of each component and explain how the processor, memory, storage and buses work together.

docs.title: The Fetch–Execute Cycle
docs.text:
What you need to know

Describe the stages of the fetch–execute cycle and the roles of the processor, registers, buses and main memory.

A program is stored in main memory as a sequence of instructions. The processor retrieves and processes one instruction at a time using the fetch–execute cycle.

The cycle has three main stages:

  1. Fetch the next instruction from memory.
  2. Decode the instruction to determine what operation is required.
  3. Execute the instruction.

The cycle repeats until the program ends or the processor is interrupted.

docs.title: Video explanation
docs.text:
This video follows an instruction through the complete fetch–decode–execute cycle and shows how the processor's registers and buses are used at each stage.

While you watch

Note what happens to the program counter, how the address, data and control buses are used, and where the fetched instruction is stored.

docs.title: Fetch
docs.text:
During the fetch stage:

  1. The program counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction.
  2. The processor places this address on the address bus.
  3. The control unit sends a read signal on the control bus.
  4. Memory sends the instruction to the processor on the data bus.
  5. The instruction is copied into the instruction register (IR).
  6. The program counter is updated so it refers to the next instruction.

docs.title: Decode
docs.text: The control unit examines the instruction in the instruction register. It identifies the operation to perform and any data or memory address required.

docs.title: Execute
docs.text:
The processor carries out the decoded instruction. This might involve:

  • performing a calculation or comparison in the ALU;
  • moving data between registers and memory;
  • reading input or producing output; or
  • changing the program counter to branch to another instruction.

The result may be stored in a register or written to memory before the next cycle begins.

A simple fetch

Suppose the program counter contains address 1023.

The processor places 1023 on the address bus and sends a read signal. Memory returns the instruction stored at that address on the data bus. The instruction is placed in the instruction register, decoded and executed. The processor then begins fetching the next instruction.

Real processors

Modern processors can overlap stages and process several instructions at once using techniques such as pipelining. The fetch–decode–execute model still explains the purpose of the cycle.

docs.title: Factors Affecting System Performance
docs.text:
What you need to know

Explain how processor clock speed, number of cores, data-bus width and cache affect system performance.

System performance depends on how quickly the computer can process instructions and move required data. No single specification guarantees that one computer will be faster than another: processor design, software, memory, storage and workload all matter.

docs.text:

While you watch

Note how each factor affects performance and why a single processor specification cannot provide a complete comparison.

docs.title: Processor clock speed
docs.text:
The processor uses regular electrical pulses to coordinate its operations. Clock speed is the number of clock cycles completed each second and is measured in hertz (Hz).

Modern processor speeds are commonly stated in gigahertz (GHz):

1 GHz = 1,000,000,000 clock cycles per second

A higher clock speed means that a processor can complete more cycles per second. When comparing otherwise similar processors, this can improve performance. However, different processor designs may complete different amounts of work per cycle, so clock speed alone is not a reliable comparison between unrelated processors.

docs.title: Processor cores
docs.text:
A multi-core processor contains two or more processing cores in one package. Each core can execute its own sequence of instructions.

Name Number of cores Dual-core 2 Quad-core 4 Hexa-core 6 Octa-core 8

Multiple cores allow suitable tasks to run in parallel. This can improve multitasking and speed up software designed to divide work between cores.

Core count is not a multiplier

A quad-core 3 GHz processor does not run one program at 12 GHz. Each core runs at its stated clock speed, and performance improves only when work can be divided efficiently.

docs.title: Data-bus width
docs.text:
The width of the data bus is the number of bits it can transfer at the same time.

  • A 32-bit data bus can transfer 32 bits in one transfer.
  • A 64-bit data bus can transfer 64 bits in one transfer.

With otherwise comparable systems, a wider data bus can move more data per transfer and reduce the number of transfers required. Actual performance also depends on bus speed, memory speed and whether the processor needs that amount of data.

32-bit and 64-bit systems

The labels 32-bit and 64-bit can also describe a processor's registers, instruction set or memory-address size. They do not always refer only to the physical width of one bus.

docs.title: Cache memory
docs.text:
Cache is smaller and faster than RAM. It keeps copies of instructions and data that the processor is likely to use soon.

When the processor needs an item:

  1. It checks the cache.
  2. If the item is present, a cache hit occurs and it can be accessed quickly.
  3. If the item is absent, a cache miss occurs. The item must be retrieved from a slower level of memory and a copy may be placed in the cache.

Cache works because programs often reuse the same data or access instructions and data stored close together.

docs.title: Cache levels
docs.text:
Processors commonly use several cache levels:

Level General characteristics L1 Smallest and fastest; normally located within each core. L2 Larger but usually slower than L1; may belong to one core or be shared. L3 Larger again and usually shared by several cores; slower than L1 and L2 but faster than RAM.

docs.title: Comparing systems fairly
docs.text: Performance claims should be based on an appropriate test or benchmark, not a single specification. A fair comparison uses the same task, software settings and conditions on each system.
